PLANT GUIDE · THE RED SIAM

Aglaonema ‘Siam Aurora’

Aglaonema ‘Siam Aurora’ — the red Chinese evergreen

A Chinese evergreen turned all the way up: lance leaves poured in red-pink, finished with a thin green rim and a whisper of the olive speckle the color was bred from. In strong light the whole crown reads red; the paler lower leaves are yesterday’s growth in yesterday’s light. Bred in Thailand, grown everywhere — and in your dot-painted pot, unmistakably yours.

🔍 Anatomy — Naming a Red Aglaonema Honestly

YOURS — red blade, thin
green rim, lance leaf
THE CLASSIC — green blade,
lipstick-red rim
‘RED ANJAMANI’ — broader,
deeper red, greener veins

The genus is certain — the lance blade, the pale midrib, and the crown of leaves on green stems are pure Aglaonema. The cultivar took real work. Your plant matches ‘Siam Aurora’ in its red form: the red covers almost the whole blade, but the thin green margin survives, and up close (see your photo card below) olive-green speckles still push in at the edges — the classic green pattern showing through the red. The nearest rival, ‘Red Anjamani’, runs broader and deeper red with green veins across the whole blade; ‘Super Red’ types lose the green rim almost entirely. One honest note: red aglaonema names get swapped freely in the trade, so this name rests on the leaves themselves, not on any nursery tag.

🌅 The name story. “Siam” is Thailand, where this cultivar was bred; “Aurora” is dawn — for the sunrise coloring. The red was bred in from Aglaonema rotundum, the one naturally red species, crossed into A. commutatum lines.

🌤️ Conditions — Forest Floor, Full Color

Aglaonemas are rainforest-floor plants built for low light — but the red is the exception. Red pigment is light-made: in dim corners a red aglaonema quietly reverts toward green, while in bright indirect light it holds the full flame. Yours is doing it right — the red crown sits where the light is, and the pale leaves underneath are simply older, shaded growth.

🪴 Care Card

☀️ LightMedium to bright indirect, ~5,000–15,000 lux (roughly 500–1,500 foot-candles). Tolerates low light but the red fades; harsh midday sun scorches.
💧 WaterWhen the top 1–2 inches of mix are dry, soak until it drains, then empty the saucer. Slightly dry beats soggy.
🚰 Water qualitySensitive to fluoride and chlorine — brown leaf tips are the tell. Distilled, rain, or water left standing overnight keeps the edges clean.
❄️ ColdKeep above 59°F. Chilling injury is real and fast — a day near 55°F can damage a third of the leaf area. Away from winter windows and AC drafts.
🪴 SoilPeat- or coir-based aroid mix with perlite for air; pH 6.0–7.5. Snug pot, drainage hole, repot only when roots crowd.
🌱 FeedingBalanced fertilizer at label strength every 4–6 weeks in spring and summer; pause in winter.

🌱 Propagation & Troubleshooting

  1. Divide first: at repotting, tease the clump apart — every offset with its own roots is a new plant.
  2. Stem cuttings: 4–6 inch pieces with at least 2 nodes, into moist mix or water at 72–76°F.
  3. Wait: roots in 3–5 weeks; pot up when roots reach 2 inches.
🌿 Red fading to greenNot enough light. Move brighter (no direct noon sun) — new leaves come back red.
🤎 Brown tipsFluoride, salts, or dry air. Switch water, flush the pot, raise humidity.
💛 Yellowing leavesOverwatering first suspect — check the roots, let the mix breathe.
🥶 Sudden collapseCold damage below 59°F — leaves go limp and dark. Warm room, trim the ruined leaves.
🕷️ PestsMealybug, scale, spider mites. Quarantine, wipe with alcohol, neem or insecticidal soap.
🐈
Not safe for animals. Aglaonema is on the ASPCA toxic list — insoluble calcium oxalate crystals. Chewing brings mouth pain, drooling, and vomiting. Keep it up out of reach. ASPCA Poison Control: (888) 426-4435.
